issue.title: _evalcache forks md5 on every call, eats most of the cached time
issue.body:
Every `_evalcache` call computes the cache key by piping into `md5` (or `md5sum`):

https://github.com/mroth/evalcache/blob/d6973f8/evalcache.plugin.zsh#L24-L28

That's a fork + exec per call, on every shell startup, even when the cache is warm. On macOS it costs ~5-7 ms each, which is kinda the whole point of the plugin tbh: the README benchmarks show cached inits at ~6-10 ms, so most of that is the hash itself.

Quick repro, 4 cached tools (starship, zoxide, fzf, brew), warm cache, `zsh -f`, 100 runs with hyperfine (M1 Pro, macOS, zsh 5.9):

| | median | p25-p75 |
|---|---|---|
| current master (d6973f8) | 64 ms | 57-72 |
| key hashed in pure zsh | 33 ms | 30-37 |
| bare `zsh -f` | 14 ms | |

So ~30 ms of a 4-tool setup is just `md5` startup.

Side bug: when neither `md5` nor `md5sum` is on PATH, every key falls back to `nohash`, so different args for the same command share one cache file:

```zsh
PATH=/bin zsh -fc 'source evalcache.plugin.zsh; _evalcache echo "echo a"; _evalcache echo "echo b"'
# prints "a" twice, both calls hit init-echo-nohash.sh
```

Proposed fix: compute the key with a tiny djb2 loop in zsh. Same inputs as today (args + function definition from #9), no fork, no external tool. It's ~0.03 ms for a typical command line. Only catch: cache filenames change, so everyone re-caches once after updating.

Happy to open a PR, got it ready.

issue.title: Keep extracted auto-import packages across cancelled builds

labels.name: repo-0441092b
labels.description: PR for untriaged, rejected, closed or missing bug

issue.body:
Fixes #65410

While typing, the auto-import warm-up gets cancelled on every keystroke and used to throw away every package it had already extracted, so it kept re-reading and re-parsing `node_modules` from scratch and never finished if you type faster than one full build. This keeps per-package extraction results on the registry, shared from one clone to the next, so a cancelled build leaves its finished packages for the next one:

- a package extraction that has started runs to completion even if the build gets cancelled, and concurrent builds wait on the in-flight one instead of starting it again (single-flight per realpath + package name + directory-search flag). New packages still aren't started after cancellation.
- the kept results get dropped as soon as anything under `node_modules` changes, any file is created or deleted, a `package.json` changes, bucket build preferences or project-reference outputs change, and once a build completes, so memory goes back to what it was once the index is ready.
- other edits are logged per snapshot generation. Each kept extraction remembers the generation that produced it and every file it read (entrypoints, alias-resolved files, project-reference sources), and it's only reused if none of those files, nor anything under the package dir, changed between the two generations. That also covers a cancelled build finishing a package after an edit already landed.

| recharts `src/cartesian/Line.tsx`, 120 keystrokes at 150 ms, diagnostics + semantic tokens per key | `main` (7 runs) | this PR (3 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| process CPU over 18 s of typing | 42.6–44.8 s | 13.5–14.0 s (−68%), 13.7–13.8 s after review fixes |
| first completion after typing stops | 217–257 ms (index never got built) | 11–13 ms (index ready) |
| `textDocument/diagnostic` median | 53–55 ms | 47.5–50 ms |
| completion-heavy typing (completion + diag + semantic tokens per key), CPU | ~17.9 s | ~17.5–17.9 s (no change) |

Measured with this harness: https://gist.github.com/hood/506e87027c83bbec1b44c1f687273349

```sh
TYPING_DIR=<recharts> TYPING_FILE=src/cartesian/Line.tsx TYPING_LINE=408 \
  TYPING_ONLY=diagnostic,semanticTokens TYPING_INTERVAL=150ms TYPING_REPS=2 TYPING_POSTCOMPLETE=1 \
  ./lspbench -test.run TestTypingBench
```

Tests:
- new `TestCancelledBuildKeepsExtractedPackages`: a build cancelled mid-extraction doesn't extract that package again on the next build (fails on `main`), and a `node_modules` change still re-extracts it.
- new `TestCancelledBuildTracksExtractionDependencies`: a workspace package re-exporting `../shared` gets re-extracted when `shared` changes after a cancelled build.
- new `TestPartialExtractionsInvalidation`: deterministic interleavings (older build publishing after an edit, edits outside the package root, unrelated edits, sibling snapshots, replacement set after a prefs change).
- completion lists are identical to `main` on the same session across 13 prefixes: 21,610 items, 6,335 of them auto-imports.
- `go test ./...`, `npx hereby lint` and `npx hereby check:format` pass.

AI disclosure: I polished my solution, my breakdown of it and -most importantly- did most of the measurements with help from an AI agent. I've gone 2x through everything and I'll handle any follow-up myself ofc.

issue.title: perf(git): cache Apple git's installation config path
issue.body:
#### Description

Caches Git's installation config path for Apple's `/usr/bin/git`, so stock macOS stops spawning `git` on every prompt. **`starship prompt` with Apple git: 63.3 ms → 40.9 ms.**

gix finds the installation config by running `git config -lz --show-origin`. Recent gitoxide (GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3182, GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3188) infers it without git for Homebrew and Linux distro git, but leaves Apple's `xcrun` shim to git on purpose. That's the one case cached here:

- only on macOS, when `git` in the prompt's `PATH` resolves to `/usr/bin/git`
- skipped when `DEVELOPER_DIR`, `GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM` or `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` is set
- stored in `$STARSHIP_CACHE/git-installation-config`, keyed by the mtime of `/var/db/xcode_select_link` (changes on `xcode-select -s`), passed to gix via `Options::git_installation_config_path()`
- the cached path must still exist, otherwise it's rediscovered; a missing config isn't cached
- written via temp file + rename, so concurrent prompts never read a partial file

| git first in `PATH` | gix 0.90 (`main`) | gix `main` branch | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Homebrew | 39.4 ms | 38.2 ms | 38.7 ms |
| Apple `/usr/bin/git` | 63.3 ms | 63.3 ms | **40.9 ms** |

`hyperfine -N -w 5 -r 40`, macOS arm64, release build, empty config, starship repo.

ahead/behind via gitoxide was split out, it'll use `Repository::ahead_behind_counts()` (GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3036) once released.

#### Motivation and Context

Closes #7850

#### How Has This Been Tested?

- `cargo test`: 1328 passed. `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -D warnings` and `cargo fmt` are clean.
- New tests: cache hit/miss/invalidation, missing config not cached, invalid cache content, non-Apple git left to gix, and an end-to-end Apple shim test on macOS.
- Prompt output is byte-identical to `main`.

- [x] I have tested using **MacOS**
- [ ] I have tested using **Linux**
- [ ] I have tested using **Windows**

#### AI-Assistance

- [x] Yes
- [ ] No

AI-assisted profiling and review. Reviewed, benchmarked and tested by me.

#### Checklist:

- [x] I have updated the documentation accordingly. (no user-facing change)
- [x] I have updated the tests accordingly.
- [x] I understand and have read the code I contribute and can answer questions about it.

comment.body:
Thanks, makes sense. Split and reworked:

**ahead/behind**: dropped from this PR. Turns out gitoxide already landed `Repository::ahead_behind_counts()` (GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3036), so nothing to upstream there. I'll open a separate PR switching to it once a gix release ships it.

**cache**: I tried gix main first (it includes Byron's GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3182, which infers the installation config without running git). Results, `starship prompt`, 40 runs, median:

| git first in `PATH` | gix 0.90 | gix main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Homebrew | 39.4 ms | 38.2 ms | 38.7 ms |
| Apple `/usr/bin/git` | 63.3 ms | 63.3 ms | **40.9 ms** |

So gix main handles Homebrew fine, but deliberately leaves Apple's `xcrun` shim to git (`gix-path/src/env/non_windows.rs`), and that spawn is ~22ms per prompt on stock macOS.

Debian without `/etc/gitconfig` (the default there) also still spawned with gix main, so I sent that upstream: GitoxideLabs/gitoxide#3188.

The cache is now scoped to the one case gix can't do cheaply: macOS, `git` resolving to `/usr/bin/git`, no `DEVELOPER_DIR`/`GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM`/`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM`. Everything else goes straight to gix. Also dropped the negative cache and the Windows bits, they aren't needed anymore.

Re finding the git binary with gix: `gix::path::env::exe_invocation()` is just `git` on Unix, so there's nothing to resolve there. I'm using `which::which_in` with the prompt's `PATH` instead.

issue.title: Reduce per-keystroke highlighting latency
issue.body:
## Summary

Reduces per-keystroke highlighting latency by 33-48% (p50) on typical command lines on my machine. Highlighting output is unchanged.

Note: my machine runs endpoint security agents that make file opens slow (`open("/dev/null")` + `close` costs 60µs in plain C). That inflates the redirection costs below, so on a clean system the gain will be smaller. The `sysread` gain does not depend on it and was reproduced by @ccjmne on another machine (21-45%).

The line counting fix and the daemon exit on early disconnect, originally part of this PR, were merged in #114 and #115.

Most of the time per keystroke went to the Zsh client, not the daemon: for a typical command line, the daemon needs 80-290µs while the whole round trip took 0.5-1.5ms.

## Where the time went

| Cost per keystroke | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `zsocket ... 2>/dev/null` | ~200µs | ~25µs |
| `{ print ... } >&$fd` when sending the request | ~120µs | single `print -u` |
| Reading spans with `read -r` (one byte per syscall) | ~8µs per span | one bulk `sysread` |
| First highlight of a new construct after daemon start | up to 1.5ms | ~0.2ms |

On my machine (macOS, zsh 5.9), any redirection on a builtin costs ~120µs, regardless of shell options, mostly because of the slow `open()`:

```
:                       3.6us
: 2>/dev/null         138.3us
: 2>&$fd               75.8us
: 2>&-                 28.9us
```

## Changes

**Client (`templates/zsh-patina.zsh`)**

- Remove the redirections from the hot path
- Send the request with a single write, and answer each CAL/NMD query with a single write
- After the first span line, read the rest of the response with `sysread` and split it into lines (see the discussion below about the protocol specification)

**Daemon (`src/daemon.rs`)**

- Wrap the response writer in a `BufWriter`. The query functions already flush before reading an answer, so the protocol is unchanged.
- Warm up with a command line that touches many more syntax contexts. Syntect compiles regexes lazily, so the first use of a construct (quotes, `$(...)`, loops, heredocs, etc.) took up to 1.5ms. The warm-up runs in the background and costs ~44ms more CPU at startup.

## Results

`main` vs this PR, client and daemon, called alternately with the same buffer, median of 400 runs, macOS, zsh 5.9:

| Command | Spans | `main` | This PR | Gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ls` | 1 | 376µs | 212µs | 44% |
| `echo hello world` | 2 | 401µs | 244µs | 39% |
| `carg` (missing command) | 1 | 657µs | 365µs | 44% |
| `git commit -m "..." && cargo build ... \| tail -3` | 20 | 808µs | 457µs | 43% |
| `for f in ~/Documents/*.txt; do ...; done` | 31 | 868µs | 451µs | 48% |
| long `docker run ...` | 13 | 794µs | 532µs | 33% |

A second run gave 35-48%.

## Testing

- `cargo test`
- `region_highlight` output is identical to `main` in 29 end-to-end cases: aliases (including recursive ones), named directories, multi-line buffers, `PREBUFFER`, active region, Unicode, history expansion

## Trade-off

If the daemon dies but leaves its socket file behind, `zsocket` now prints its own error to stderr in addition to the existing `zle -M` message. This only affects that failure path.

## AI usage

Claude Code (Opus 5.5) built profiling harnesses and helped with profiling, then reviewed the code and ran a parallel run of the benchmarks to ensure results matched with manual ones.

comment.body:
Thanks @ccjmne, super useful, and not dismissive at all!

**4 (`whence`)**: you're right, dropped it in 94c8178. Back to `whence -p`. Your numbers made me dig a bit, and tbh the ~120µs per redirection is kinda my machine, not macOS. It runs a couple of endpoint security agents (company laptop), and a plain C loop shows it:

| Syscall | My machine |
|---|---|
| `open("/dev/null")` + `close` | 60µs |
| `dup` + `close` | 11µs |
| `getppid` | 0.12µs |

So file opens are what's slow here, and that's what made `whence ... >/dev/null 2>&1` look so expensive. On a clean system the gain from removing redirections is gonna be much smaller. It's never slower though, so I kept those changes, and I fixed the description so it doesn't oversell them.

**5 (`sysread`)**: thanks for running it, glad the trend holds on your side too. Waiting for your take ofc. To anticipate the protocol concern: today the daemon sends all `CAL`/`NMD` queries before the first span (`resolve_callables` runs before the span loop in `handle_highlight`), so this works. But §7.1.5 allows interleaving, and with a future daemon that sends a query after a span, the client would wait for EOF while the daemon waits for an answer. The keystroke would hang until the 1s read timeout. That's the footgun, I think.

If that's a blocker, two options I'd see:

1. **Tighten the spec** so the daemon must send all query blocks before the first span line. That's what it already does, so nothing changes in practice, and the client can keep the bulk read.
2. **Keep the spec and make the client handle it**: after each `sysread` chunk, check whether a line starting with `?` arrived (`[[ $rest == (\?*|*$'\n'\?*) ]]`). If not, keep reading in bulk. If yes, hand the buffered lines to the existing query handler, answer, and continue. A bit more code, but it costs almost nothing when there are no late queries.

I'd lean towards 1 tbh, but happy to do 2 if you'd rather keep the freedom in the protocol.

issue.title: Reading line-oriented input clears a 4 KiB buffer for every line
issue.body:
`jq_util_input_read_more()` clears the whole 4 KiB input buffer with `memset(state->buf, 0xff, sizeof(state->buf))` before every `fgets()` call ([src/util.c:300](https://github.com/jqlang/jq/blob/5c001b18d7237cce1fdba63608732163f978dd23/src/util.c#L300)). Input is read one line at a time, so pretty-printed JSON (GitHub API responses, `kubectl get -o json`, anything saved from `jq .`) pays for a 4 KiB memset per line, while those lines are ~22 bytes on average. Same goes for `-R` on short lines.

The memset is there so the length of a read that ends without a newline can be found by scanning back for the NUL `fgets()` writes. Only the bytes written by the previous read can differ from 0xff tho, so resetting just those is enough.

**To Reproduce**

```sh
cat > gen.jq <<'EOF'
[range(10000) | {id: ., node_id: "MDEwOlJlcG9zaXRvcnk\(.)", name: "repo-\(.)", full_name: "org\(. % 50)/repo-\(.)", private: (. % 10 == 0), owner: {login: "user\(. % 997)", id: (. * 7), type: "User", site_admin: false}, html_url: "https://github.com/org\(. % 50)/repo-\(.)", description: "a small description of repository number \(.)", stargazers_count: (. * 37 % 50000), topics: ["cli", "json"], license: {key: "mit", name: "MIT License"}}]
EOF
jq -nc -f gen.jq > compact.json   # 3.9 MB, 1 line
jq . compact.json > pretty.json   # 5.4 MB, 240k lines
hyperfine -N 'jq length compact.json' 'jq length pretty.json'
```

The same data takes 53 ms compact vs 100 ms pretty-printed on macOS, and 60 ms vs 92 ms on Linux. The memset is 11-13 ms of that gap, ~76M of the 1.1G instructions callgrind counts for the pretty file. The rest is per-byte parser work, which open PRs like #3718 already cover.

**Environment**

- macOS 27 arm64 (Apple clang), Debian trixie arm64 (gcc 14) in Docker
- jq master at 5c001b1

I've got a small fix with a test, will open a PR.

issue.title: Reuse diagnostics checker for semantic tokens of checked files

labels.name: repo-0441092b
labels.description: PR for untriaged, rejected, closed or missing bug

issue.body:
Fixes #65386

Semantic tokens used to run on a cold query checker and re-infer basically every variable, parameter and property type in the file, the same work diagnostics had just done on the diagnostics checker. With this PR, once a diagnostics request has fully checked a file and is done, semantic tokens for that file borrow the idle diagnostics checker instead.

The rules are kinda strict so the diagnostics checker's walk order doesn't change:
- it's only lent out if it's idle (non-blocking `diagSem`), the file is fully checked (`typeChecked` + `unusedChecked`, not cancelled) and no diagnostics request for that file is still in flight (they acquire it three times: semantic, suggestion, declaration);
- otherwise semantic tokens get a query checker exactly like today, and they never wait.

That ordering is what avoids stuff like #51661, where a query asked for a type before the normal walk and you'd get an order-dependent false error in the editor.

VSCode pulls diagnostics right on change (`diagnosticPullOptions.onChange`) and only asks for semantic tokens ≥300 ms later (`REQUEST_MIN_DELAY`), so in practice the reuse path is the common one.

| recharts `src/cartesian/Line.tsx`, 120 keystrokes, 3 runs | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| diagnostics then semantic tokens: `semanticTokens/full` median | 41.3–41.7 ms | 2.88–2.91 ms (−93%) |
| same: `textDocument/diagnostic` median | 52.6–53.2 ms | 52.4–52.9 ms |
| same: process CPU | 14.5–14.7 s | 8.6 s (−41%) |
| both sent together: keystroke median / CPU | 53–55 ms / 14.7 s | 54 ms / 14.7 s (falls back, no change) |

Tests:
- new `TestCheckerPoolCheckedFileQuery` covers no reuse before the file is checked, no reuse while the diagnostics request is still in flight, reuse after, and fallback while the checker is lent out. It fails if the in-flight guard gets removed.
- semantic tokens + diagnostics for `Line.tsx` and three other open files (TS2883 type printing, unused suggestions, the transient errors you get mid-typing) are byte-identical to `main` across 600 responses, both sequential and concurrent.
- `go test ./...`, `npx hereby lint` and `npx hereby check:format` pass.

One thing I'm not 100% sure about: after the file is checked, classification still creates a few types/symbols on the diagnostics checker (~6 types and 32 symbols per request here, looks like throwaway re-checks of expressions). I didn't see any diagnostics change, but if keeping that checker totally free of query work is a hard requirement this approach doesn't fit, so happy to go another way.

AI disclosure: I polished my solution, my breakdown of it and -most importantly- did most of the measurements with help from an AI agent. I've gone 2x through everything and I'll handle any follow-up myself ofc.

comment.body:
Yeah that's fair, tbh I couldn't fully convince myself either: even with the guard, classification still creates a handful of types/symbols on the borrowed checker (~6/32 per request on recharts' `Line.tsx`), and those could run before another file's check. So it's only "safe" for the cases I diffed, not in general.

Converting this to a draft and parking it behind #65064 (happy to just close it if you prefer). If order independence lands, the payoff is roughly: in VS Code's request order, semantic tokens go 41 → 3 ms per request and ~41% less CPU while typing, since today each edit type-checks the file twice.

If it's useful, I've got a small LSP typing harness (real keystrokes on a real repo, pulls diagnostics/semantic tokens/completions per key, dumps responses for byte-identity diffs): https://gist.github.com/hood/506e87027c83bbec1b44c1f687273349. Switched it to `MarshalJSONTo`, so the wrapped message gets encoded straight into the encoder. | `BenchmarkMarshalCompletionResponse` (2k items, n=10) | 1.934 ms ±7% | 1.273 ms ±1% | −34.2% (p=0.000) |
| B/op | 1243 KiB | 467 KiB | −62.5% |
| allocs/op | 37 | 16 | −57% |
| completion in `recharts` `Line.tsx` (531 KB) | 2.93 ms | 1.89 ms | −36% |

```sh
go -C ./tsc test -run '^$' -bench MarshalCompletionResponse -count 10 ./internal/lsp/lsproto
```

issue.title: Auto-import warm-up restarts from scratch on every keystroke while typing

labels.name: repo-0441092b
labels.description: This issue needs a team member to investigate its status.

issue.body:
### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

**Summary:** while we type, the language server keeps rebuilding the auto-import index in the background and throwing the work away. Every keystroke cancels the warm-up and starts a new one from scratch, which re-reads and re-parses `node_modules` each time. By typing faster than one full build takes (>~400 ms on a reasonably sized app), it never finishes and just keeps burning a couple of cores.

**Where** (`main` @ 1623a1991)

- `Session.warmAutoImportCache` (`project/session.go:2080`) starts building the registry after every single-file snapshot change.
- `DidChangeFile` cancels it right away on the next keystroke (`project/session.go:378`).
- Finished packages live in `extractionCache`, which is local to one build (`ls/autoimport/registry.go:921`). Cancelling a build drops all of them, and a "big" package (e.g. `lodash`/`d3`/`react types`) can take longer than the gap between keystrokes on its own, so it never gets done.

It hits whenever we type without triggering completions: comments, strings, JSX text, clients that don't ask for completions on every keystroke, and the first seconds after opening a project. A completion request builds the index synchronously and stops the waste, but it can get cancelled the same way.

**Measured** (Apple M1 Pro, on `recharts`'s `src/cartesian/Line.tsx` file: 1,093 lines in a 658-file repo; 120 keystrokes at 150 ms each, pulling diagnostics + semantic tokens after every keystroke)

| | `main` (7 runs) | with the fix below (3 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| process CPU over 18 s of typing | 42.6–44.8 s | 13.5–14.0 s (−68%) |
| first completion after typing stops | 217–257 ms (index never got built) | 11–13 ms (index ready) |
| `textDocument/diagnostic` median | 53–55 ms | 47.5–50 ms |

A CPU profile of a semantic-tokens-only session (on `f7973164a`, same code in these files) shows 10.3 s of `ReadFile` syscalls in a 6.9 s run, nearly all from `autoImportBuilderFS` re-reading package files 🫠.

**Possible fix** (already in my proposal branch: hood/TypeScript `perf/autoimport-partial-extraction`, one file + tests)

Keep per-package extraction results on the registry, shared from one clone to the next, so a cancelled build still leaves its finished packages for the next attempt:
- a package extraction that has already started finishes even if the build gets cancelled, concurrent builds wait on the in-flight extraction instead of starting it again, and new packages still aren't started after cancellation.
- the kept results are dropped as soon as any file under `node_modules`, or under a kept package's own directory, changes (workspace packages), when the build preferences or project-reference outputs change, and once a build completes.

On the same session, the completion lists are identical to `main` for 13 different prefixes: 21,610 items, 6,335 of them auto-imports. Completion-heavy typing (completion + diagnostics + semantic tokens on every keystroke) stays basically the same at ~17.9 s CPU on both. Sanity checked with tests, and the full Go suite passes. Note that I also added new tests to cover reusing packages extracted before a cancellation and re-extracting after a `node_modules` change.

Happy to open a PR if this approach sounds right to you, or change it if you'd rather handle it differently, e.g. start the warm-up only after an idle pause.

AI disclosure: I polished my solution, my breakdown of it and -most importantly- did most of the measurements with help from an AI agent. I've gone 2x through everything and I'll handle any follow-up myself ofc.

perf(pacquet): avoid nested tarball extraction parallelism without regressions
issue.body:
## Problem

On a cold frozen install of the pinned Next.js workspace from https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13305, the TypeScript CLI completed in 11.30s while the Rust CLI completed in 13.84s on the same machine and dependency graph.

Investigation indicates that many tarballs are downloaded concurrently while each tarball with at least 32 files also uses inner parallel extraction. This nested parallelism increases scheduling and filesystem contention. As an experiment, effectively disabling per-tarball parallel extraction improved Rust fetch performance, but applying that globally could regress workloads with one or a few very large tarballs.

The concurrent integrity/extraction benchmark added by https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/13433 provides a deterministic regression workload for the many-tarball case.

## Proposed investigation

Test an adaptive, globally bounded extraction strategy rather than simply increasing or removing `PARALLEL_EXTRACT_THRESHOLD`:

- preserve inner parallel extraction when only a few large tarballs are active;
- prefer sequential extraction within each tarball when many tarballs are already in flight;
- prevent outer package concurrency from multiplying unboundedly with per-tarball file concurrency.

Before choosing an implementation, parameterize the integrity benchmark across:

- 1, 8, 32, 128, and 256 concurrent tarballs;
- 8, 32, 64, 256, and 2,048 files per tarball;
- small and large files;
- compressible and incompressible content.

## End-to-end validation

Validate baseline Rust against candidate Rust on:

1. The pinned Next.js cold frozen-install reproduction.
2. All 48 installation scenarios from https://github.com/vltpkg/benchmarks/pull/132:
   - fixtures: Next.js, Astro, Svelte, Vue, Large, and Babylon.js;
   - states: clean, cache, cache plus lockfile, cache plus `node_modules`, cache plus lockfile plus `node_modules`, lockfile, lockfile plus `node_modules`, and `node_modules`.
3. The vlt `build`, `build-cache`, and `run` scenarios as correctness checks.
4. Single-large-tarball microbenchmarks that exercise the workload most likely to benefit from inner parallel extraction.

Run at least five measured iterations after warmup. Repeat apparent regressions with baseline/candidate order reversed so machine drift is not mistaken for an implementation effect.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Next.js cold frozen install improves by at least 10%.
- The concurrent-tarball microbenchmark improves materially.
- No repeatable vlt installation scenario regresses by more than 3%.
- Single-large-tarball scenarios do not regress by more than 3%.
- Aggregate vlt performance does not regress.
- Package counts, exit codes, lockfiles, and installed dependency graphs remain equivalent.

The optimization should not be merged if it only exchanges the Next.js regression for a regression in low-concurrency or large-tarball workloads.

---
Written by an agent (Codex, GPT-5).

comment.body:
Some macOS data for this one. The nested fan-out shows up there too, mostly as system time rather than wall time.

**Setup:** pnpm 12.18.0 built from pnpm/pnpm@3600b05d00, M1 Pro (10 cores), APFS. Fixture is the integrated-benchmark one (1356 snapshots, ~33k files). Cold store, `install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` against registry.npmjs.org. The machine runs an EDR (Carbon Black plus a JumpCloud ES extension), so absolute syscall costs are inflated. That's pretty common on corporate dev Macs tbh.

## Cold install

| run | wall | user | sys |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11.6 s | 2.2 s | 31.6 s |
| 2 | 11.0 s | 2.2 s | 28.1 s |
| 3 | 9.4 s | 2.1 s | 29.1 s |

`pnpm fetch` (store only) alone is 24.6 s sys, so almost all of it is the store write, not linking.

## The global rayon pool isn't the cause

| `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` | wall (2 runs) | sys |
|---|---|---|
| 16 (default here) | 12.9 / 10.6 s | 25.1 / 27.9 s |
| 8 | 9.3 / 8.5 s | 27.4 / 26.7 s |
| 4 | 9.0 / 9.0 s | 27.2 / 27.4 s |
| 2 | 9.4 / 8.6 s | 27.0 / 27.9 s |

Sys stays at ~27 s whatever the rayon size. The wall numbers are network-noisy, so I wouldn't read much into them.

## Who's in the kernel

Thread census mid-install: 40 `tokio-rt-worker` (10 async plus ~30 blocking from [`post_download_semaphore`](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/3600b05d0069990995ef418079eb5b8a0cfb00de/pnpm/crates/tarball/src/lib.rs#L108) and [`streaming_extract_semaphore`](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/3600b05d0069990995ef418079eb5b8a0cfb00de/pnpm/crates/tarball/src/lib.rs#L124)), 10 [`cas-write`](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/3600b05d0069990995ef418079eb5b8a0cfb00de/pnpm/crates/tarball/src/lib.rs#L143), 16 global rayon, 4 `pnpm-link`.

`sample` over 7 s of a cold install, thread-ms on the leaf syscall (symbolized build):

| pool | syscall | thread-ms | caller |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cas-write` | `open` | 5861 | `StoreDir::write_cas_file` |
| blocking (`BufferedExtraction::run`) | `open` | 2297 | `StoreDir::write_cas_file` |
| `cas-write` + blocking | `write` | 2636 | `StoreDir::write_cas_file` |
| `cas-write` + blocking | `close` | 2635 | `StoreDir::write_cas_file` |
| `pnpm-link` | `clonefileat` | 3315 | `link_file::clone_tier`, `dir_clone_cache` |
| `cas-write` + blocking | `stat` (parent dir) | 487 | `unix_creation_mode` |
| `cas-write` + blocking | `fstat` | 343 | `grant_mode_bits` |

A create-`open` costs ~250 µs here vs ~100 µs for a per-file `clonefileat`. So ~40 threads are queueing on the metadata path that `dir_clone_cache.rs` already describes as serialized volume-wide, and the queueing is what burns the sys time.

## Takeaways for the design

- On macOS the useful cap is on concurrent CAS *creators*: the blocking extractors that write inline under [`PARALLEL_EXTRACT_THRESHOLD`](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/3600b05d0069990995ef418079eb5b8a0cfb00de/pnpm/crates/tarball/src/extract.rs#L292) plus the `cas-write` pool, not the rayon pool.
- A wall-time win is unproven. A cap should cut sys time a lot (laptop CPU, fans), but wall is bounded by the APFS ceiling either way. The cold-pnpr scenario is probably the right way to measure it, since the npm registry is too noisy for this.
- Side note: the per-file parent `stat` in [`unix_creation_mode`](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/3600b05d0069990995ef418079eb5b8a0cfb00de/pnpm/crates/fs/src/file_mode.rs#L370) is ~3% of CAS syscall time. The shard dirs' mode could be cached once per dir.

### Repro

```sh
cp pnpm/tasks/integrated-benchmark/src/fixtures/* /tmp/proj && cd /tmp/proj
rm -rf node_modules store-dir && /usr/bin/time -l pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts
# per-pool breakdown: build with CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=false, then
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts & sample $! 7 1 -file cold.sample
```

issue.body:
**AI-assisted contribution:** prepared with assistance from GPT and Opus. The code was adapted from nxtedition/undici#119 and validated with the tests and A/B benchmarks below.

## This relates to...

Upstream adaptation of [nxtedition/undici#119](https://github.com/nxtedition/undici/pull/119).

## Rationale

HTTP/1 response parsing currently allocates Buffer views and raw field arrays, then `Request` lowercases/decodes them into a second header map. Build that map directly in the parser and forward it to the handler, controller and diagnostics instead.

## Changes

- Both llhttp and Milo build lowercase-name maps with Latin-1 string values and arrays for duplicate field lines. Header values retain their casing and bytes.
- Intern 95 common response field names using a 32-bit byte hash and a 256-slot table. Every hit checks full hash, length and bytes; deliberate full-hash collisions are covered. `build/header-name-hash.js` reproduces the constants.
- llhttp lowercases only consumed field-name bytes in its WASM copy and decodes value ranges directly. Milo lowercases field-name ranges in its raw input. Fragmented fields, empty values, informational responses, upgrades and trailers retain their parser lifecycles.
- `Request` forwards the maps directly, without calling `parseHeaders`. HTTP/2 already supplies maps. The legacy array utilities and tree remain for explicit raw-array callers, Fetch/form-data and public utility compatibility.
- Preserve upstream's existing own-property handling of `__proto__`, constructor and other prototype-shadowing names.
- Preserve field boundaries for Connection and Keep-Alive and require complete persistence tokens and exact timeout parameter names in both engines. Close takes precedence across all repeated fields. This includes the fix from nxtedition/undici#124 and nodejs/undici#5940.
- Include regression tests and reproducible in-memory parsing/helper benchmarks, including ordinary `Map.get` after decoding/lowercasing.

### Breaking Changes and Deprecations

`controller.rawHeaders`, `controller.rawTrailers` and HTTP/1 response diagnostics now expose mutable maps rather than Buffer pairs. Names are lowercased; duplicate values are grouped in arrays, so original field-name casing and interleaving are no longer retained. ## TLDR

On every tooltip commit, `BarChart`'s `ChartCore` hands its children fresh `cloneElement` results, so **every bar chart child re-renders on hover**, including the ones that only read `useChartStable()` (`Bar`, `Grid`, `ReferenceArea`, `TrendLine`, …). > Update: #341 fixed the same problem in the time-series shell (Line / Area / Composed). `BarChart` still has it.

| Chart | Hover commits | Re-renders of a child that reads no hover state |
|---|---|---|
| `BarChart`, 24 bars, 2 series | 209 | **192** |

## Where

Hover state (`useChartInteraction`) lives in `ChartCore`, so it re-renders on each commit. In the same render, `bar-chart.tsx` re-partitions `children`: `forEachChartChild` → `renderKeyedChartLayers()` → `cloneElement` for every child. A cloned element has a new props object, so React can't bail out.

## Repro

```tsx
let renders = 0;
function Probe() {
  renders += 1;
  return null;
}

<BarChart data={data} xDataKey="name">
  <Bar dataKey="a" />
  <Probe />
  <ChartTooltip />
</BarChart>
```

`renders` goes up once per tooltip commit.

## Proposed fix

Partition and key children in a `useMemo` on `[children]`, as `classifyChartChildren` now does in the time-series shell, with the same per-render fallback while a lazy child is unresolved.

issue.body:
## Summary

On a **no-op** or **one-file rebuild**, every clean `deps = gcc|msvc` edge still copies its whole deps log entry into the graph: `LoadDepsFromLog` inserts every recorded dep inside of `edge->inputs_` and calls `AddOutEdge` on each of them (`src/graph.cc`, `ImplicitDepLoader::LoadDepsFromLog`). Since `0b115d8` deps are already skipped for dirty edges, so after a no-op build it is *only* clean edges that pay this, and clean edges never enter the plan anyway 🤷‍♂️ (`Plan::AddSubTarget` returns early on `outputs_ready()`).

On a 10k-TU project with ~800 deps per TU (typical with `-MD`, system headers included) that is ~8.5M `Node*` copied into `inputs_` plus ~8.5M `push_back`s into the `out_edges_` of a few hundred headers, each growing to ~10k entries.

macOS 15, M1 Pro, `1a8fee2`, Release build. Workload: `misc/write_fake_manifests.py -t 200` (10,533 edges, 10,250 TUs, ~830 deps per TU), built once, then `ninja` with nothing to do. | - of which `LoadDepsFromLog` (+ `memmove`/`malloc` from vector growth) | ~100 ms |

issue.title: HexDecode is scalar: Buffer.from(hex) ~5x slower than base64 decode
issue.body:
`HexDecode` decodes one byte per iteration through `unhex_table` early
exiting on the first invalid digit. 
The early exit keeps compilers from vectorizing the loop. 

For this very reason in `node`, `Buffer.from(str, 'hex')` and `buf.write(str,
'hex')` run ~5x slower than base64 decoding (which uses `simdutf`),
even though hex is the simpler format 😄.

Measuring this on Node.js v26.13.0 (official build), Apple M1 Pro, median ns/op:

| Input bytes | `Buffer.from(hex)` | `Buffer.from(base64)` |
|---|---|---|
| 256 | 266 | 132 |
| 1024 | 782 | 212 |
| 16384 | 11347 | 2068 |

The cost is all in `HexDecode`: the out-of-line function alone takes 10.4 µs
for 16 KiB for `-O3` (~0.65 ns/byte).

Just sanity checking thex existence of a "famous" consumer: Postgres `bytea`
(node-postgres decodes it with `Buffer.from(hex)`), keys and digests decoded
from hex, and ObjectId/UUID-style ids.

Proposal: decode whole 16-byte output blocks with NEON (on `arm64`) and SSE2
(on `x86-64` baseline, no SSSE3 needed), and fall back to the existing scalar
loop at the first block that contains an invalid character. The scalar loop
then finds the exact stopping point, so results stay byte-identical to today's,
including truncation at the first invalid pair. To clarify: the change only
affects one-byte input, as two-byte strings keep the scalar path.

issue.title: perf(gix): read directories ahead in `status` dirwalks
issue.body:
> This PR and its description were written by Claude Code, an AI agent, working for @hood. The measurements below are the agent's own.

### Summary

`status` with untracked files now reads directories ahead on worker threads, while the walk itself stays serial and unchanged. On a starship-like `status`, this is **38-56% faster** on everyday repositories, with byte-identical results.

**Motivation:** shell prompts. starship's `git_status` module runs `Repository::status()` with untracked files enabled, once per prompt, and that time is dominated by the directory walk: on pnpm, ~250 of the 285 ms. The walk is syscall-bound (user 0.02 s, system 0.19 s for 3,562 `read_dir` calls), so parallel reads pay off. Closes #3180.

### Changes

- **`feat(gix-dir)!`**: new `walk::Options::prefetch_threads`, defaulting to `0` (unchanged behavior).
  - When it is set, the walk collects directories with tracked files from the index (below the traversal root, ignoring `SKIP_WORKTREE` entries) and keeps one `OnceLock` per directory.
  - Scoped threads fill them in index order, and the walker calls `get_or_init()`: it uses a finished listing, waits for one in progress, or reads the directory itself. No directory is read twice.
  - Untracked and ignored directories are still read live by the walker, so ignored trees such as `node_modules` are never read ahead.
  - A failed read leaves no listing, and the walker falls back to the existing live read, so errors, `read_dir_errors` and `read_dir_calls` stay the same.
  - Walks for deletion ignore the option.
  - Corrects the performance notes of `walk()`, which said traversal is rare in typical Git usage.
- **`perf(gix)`**: `Repository::index_worktree_status()` sets `prefetch_threads` from `thread_limit` (`gix_parallel::num_threads()`, or `0` when that resolves to one thread). `Repository::dirwalk()` is unchanged.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I[index entries] --> D[sorted dirs with tracked files]
  D --> W1[prefetch thread 1]
  D --> W2[prefetch thread N]
  W1 --> L[(OnceLock per dir)]
  W2 --> L
  T[serial walker] -- get_or_init --> L
  T -- untracked / failed dirs --> R[live read_dir]
```

### Results

Starship-like `status`: untracked `Matching`, `TrackRenames::Disabled`, `thread_limit: Some(3)` (starship's macOS default) or `None`. Apple M1 Pro, macOS, hyperfine, 30 runs each, medians, local clones:

| Repository | Dirs / tracked files | `thread_limit` | `main` | This PR | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| neovim | 233 / 3,947 | 3 | 28.8 ms | 17.7 ms | **−39%** |
| vite | 946 / 2,927 | 3 | 116.6 ms | 72.4 ms | **−38%** |
| pnpm | 3,562 / 10,660 | 3 | 284.8 ms | 124.0 ms | **−56%** |
| neovim | | all cores | 34.2 ms | 19.8 ms | −42% |
| vite | | all cores | 116.8 ms | 77.1 ms | −34% |
| pnpm | | all cores | 304.7 ms | 110.2 ms | −64% |
| pnpm, no untracked (control) | | 3 | 36.8 ms | 33.0 ms | noise |

CPU time rises a little (pnpm with 3 threads: user 34 → 42 ms, system 229 → 351 ms), which is the cost of the extra reader threads.

This machine runs endpoint security software, which makes every syscall more expensive: `git status` on neovim takes ~40 ms here. Expect lower absolute times elsewhere. The relative gain depends on how expensive `read_dir` is.

### Correctness

- New test `walk::prefetching_directories_yields_the_same_outcome`. It walks every repository of the `many.sh` fixture with `prefetch_threads` `0` and `3`, across three emission configurations, with fresh and stale indices, and asserts equal entries and `Outcome`. When prefetched listings are deliberately truncated, the test fails.
- Compared sorted `status` items between `main` and this branch on a dirty pnpm worktree:
  - The tree had untracked files at several depths, new nested directories, empty directories, ignored `node_modules` at the root and nested, a symlink to a directory, and modified, deleted and type-changed tracked files.
  - Both `Matching` and collapsed emission were compared, with 3 threads and with all cores, 5 runs each.
  - Result: identical in all 20 runs (3,832 and 3,834 items).
- With `GIX_TEST_IGNORE_ARCHIVES=1`, these pass on macOS:
  - `cargo test -p gix-dir --features sha1`: 86 tests.
  - `cargo test -p gix-status --features sha1`: 42 tests.
  - `cargo test -p gix`: 682 tests.
- `cargo clippy` is clean for `-p gix-dir -p gix-status -p gix --all-targets`, and for `-p gix --no-default-features --features status,sha1`, where `gix-parallel` is serial and prefetching is off.
- `cargo +stable fmt --check` passes.

### Reproduce

The harness is a ~60-line binary depending on `gix` with `default-features = false, features = ["max-performance", "revision", "status", "sha1", "zlib-sirocco"]` (starship's set). It opens with `ThreadSafeRepository::discover_opts()` and iterates `repo.status(..)?.index_worktree_options_mut(|o| { o.thread_limit = Some(3); o.dirwalk_options.as_mut().map(|d| d.set_emit_untracked(Matching).set_emit_ignored(None).set_emit_pruned(false).set_emit_empty_directories(false)); }).tree_index_track_renames(Disabled).into_iter(None)`.

```bash
for r in neovim vite pnpm; do (cd $r && hyperfine -N -w 5 -r 30 "$MAIN status ." "$BRANCH status ."); done
```

Avoid spawning `git` to find the installation config on Unix

type.name: Feature

issue.body:
> This issue was written by Claude Code, an AI agent, working for @hood. The measurements below are the agent's own.

### Summary

With `permissions.config.git_binary` enabled, every process that opens a repository runs `git config -lz --show-origin --no-includes --show-scope --name-only` once to find the installation configuration (`gix-path/src/env/git/mod.rs`, `GIT_CONFIG_PATHS`). On Unix there is no way around the spawn, unlike the recent Windows work that finds the paths without launching Git.

For one-shot processes this spawn is the largest part of opening a repository. starship enables `git_binary` (`src/context/mod.rs`, `gix::open::permissions::Config { git_binary: true, .. }`) and runs as a new process for every prompt, so every prompt in a Git repository pays for it.

I'd like to discuss whether, and how, gitoxide could avoid it on Unix before writing any code.

### Measurements

Apple M1 Pro, macOS, upstream `576bfd2`, neovim clone, hyperfine and in-process timers:

| | Time |
|---|---|
| discover + open, `git_binary: false` | 4.6 ms |
| discover + open, `git_binary: true` | 55.8 ms |
| the spawned command alone, Homebrew Git 2.56 | 55.1 ± 12.0 ms (user 5.4 ms, system 9.7 ms) |
| the spawned command alone, `/usr/bin/git` (Apple Git, `xcrun` shim) | 92.0 ± 11.7 ms |

This machine runs endpoint security software, which inflates process creation, so absolute numbers will be lower elsewhere. Even so, a `fork`/`exec` of Git is much more than the rest of `open()`.

### What the spawn finds here

| `git` in `PATH` | Scope | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| `/opt/homebrew/bin/git` → `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/git/2.56.0_2/bin/git` | system | `/opt/homebrew/etc/gitconfig` |
| `/usr/bin/git` (Apple Git-157) | unknown | `/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/share/git-core/gitconfig` |
| typical Linux distribution Git | system | `/etc/gitconfig` |

### Options I can think of

1. **Infer the paths without Git on Unix**, like `config_paths_without_git()` on Windows. Resolve `git` in `PATH`, follow symlinks, and check known layouts: `<prefix>/etc/gitconfig` for Homebrew and distribution builds, the active developer directory's `usr/share/git-core/gitconfig` for Apple Git, and fall back to spawning when nothing matches unambiguously. The risk is a layout that matches but isn't what this Git reads. For example, `ETC_GITCONFIG` is a compile-time setting, and `RUNTIME_PREFIX` builds resolve it relative to the binary.
2. **Leave it to applications.** `open::Options::git_installation_config_path()` already lets callers pass the path. Long-lived callers pay the cost once, but one-shot callers like prompts would need their own cache, keyed by the Git executable.
3. **Use a cheaper probe.** As far as I know, Git has no cheaper way to report its installation configuration path than `git config --show-origin`. `git --exec-path` is just as expensive to spawn.

Does option 1 sound acceptable if it only applies when the result is unambiguous and otherwise falls back to the current spawn? Or should this stay with applications (option 2)?

issue.title: `status` with untracked files is bound by a serial directory walk
issue.body:
> This issue was written by Claude Code, an AI agent, working for @hood. The measurements below are the agent's own.

### Summary

`status` with untracked files enabled spends most of its wall time in the directory walk, which reads every directory serially on one thread. The walk is almost entirely system time, so it leaves the other cores idle while the index check finishes early.

This is the path a shell prompt takes on every command: starship's `git_status` module runs `Repository::status()` with untracked files on by default, once per prompt.

### Evidence

Starship-like `status` (untracked `Matching`, `thread_limit: Some(3)`, starship's macOS default), upstream `576bfd2`, Apple M1 Pro, macOS, hyperfine medians:

| Repository | Dirs | Tracked files | `status` | `status` without untracked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| neovim | 233 | 3,947 | 28.8 ms | 15.7 ms |
| vite | 946 | 2,927 | 116.6 ms | 51.6 ms |
| pnpm | 3,562 | 10,660 | 284.8 ms | 36.8 ms |

On pnpm, `gix dirwalk` alone takes 0.31 s wall with 0.02 s user and 0.19 s system time, for 3,562 `read_dir` calls. The index check runs on its own threads, so the dirwalk thread decides the total.

Directory reads parallelize well on the same tree (`fd -uu --exclude .git -t d`, pnpm):

| Threads | Wall time |
|---|---|
| 1 | 313 ms |
| 3 | 156 ms |
| 8 | 104 ms |

Where it happens:
- `gix-dir/src/walk/readdir.rs`: `recursive()` calls `gix_fs::read_dir()` for each directory, one at a time.
- `gix-dir/src/walk/function.rs`: the performance notes say parallel traversal was abandoned because "traversal is rare in typical Git usage". That no longer holds: every `status` with untracked files traverses the whole worktree.

### Proposed fix

The index already tells which directories contain tracked files, and the walk always enters those. Worker threads can read their listings ahead of time, while the traversal itself stays serial and unchanged:

- Collect directories with tracked files (below the traversal root, skipping `SKIP_WORKTREE` entries) from the index.
- Store one `OnceLock` per directory. Workers fill them, and the walker calls `get_or_init()`: it uses a finished listing, waits for one in progress, or reads the directory itself.
- Any read error falls back to the current live read, so error handling and statistics stay the same. Walks for deletion are not affected.
- Make it opt-in in `gix-dir` via `walk::Options::prefetch_threads`, and let `gix` status derive it from its `thread_limit`.

A prototype brings the numbers above to 17.7 ms (neovim, −39%), 72.4 ms (vite, −38%) and 124 ms (pnpm, −56%), with output identical to upstream. A PR follows.

issue.title: Parser bookkeeping costs ~20% of steady-state highlighting
issue.body:
## Problem

In steady-state highlighting (regexes already compiled), ~20% of the time goes to parser bookkeeping, not to regex search. Profile of highlighting `src/parsing/scope.rs` repeatedly (macOS `sample`, upstream `4efbec1`):

| Frame | Self/inclusive share |
|---|---|
| `MatchIter::next` | 11.7% |
| `MatchIter` Vec growth (`grow_one`, malloc/free from `context_iter`) | ~4% |
| `onig::Region` clone + free (`onig_region_copy`, `onig_region_free`) | ~4.5% |
| `SearchCache` insert/lookup (FNV over 8 pointer bytes) | ~3% |

For that 729-line file the parser does 6.7k tokens, 86k regex searches and 308k search-cache lookups (~46 per token, 70% of them hit a cached "no match").

## Causes

1. `context_iter` (`src/parsing/syntax_definition.rs:302`) allocates two Vecs per call, and they grow on the first `include`. `find_best_match` calls it once per context in the chain, per token.
2. `SearchCache` is keyed by `*const MatchPattern` but hashed with FNV, which runs 8 dependent multiply rounds per key.
3. `search_with_end` clones the matched `Region` into the cache and again for the caller, and clones on every cache hit, even though only the winning match is used.

## Proposed fix

1. Keep the `MatchIter` include stack inline (8 levels, spilling to a Vec beyond that). No public API change.
2. Hash the pointer key with a single multiply.
3. Track the best candidate by cache key and only materialise the winner's `Region`. A consuming winner's cache entry can't be reused (the next token starts after it), so move it out of the cache instead of cloning.

Measured on a prototype: steady-state highlighting 4.5-13% faster across Rust/JS/Python/C/Markdown/YAML files, output byte-identical.

issue.title: SyntaxSet loading decodes the lazy contexts blob one byte at a time
issue.body:
## Problem

`SyntaxSet::load_defaults_newlines()` / `load_defaults_nonewlines()` take ~1.8 ms warm (~2.7 ms on first call in a process). This is paid on every start of a CLI built on syntect (bat, delta, `syncat`), so on small files it is a large share of total runtime.

## Cause

`SyntaxReference::serialized_lazy_contexts` is a `Vec<u8>` (`src/parsing/syntax_set.rs:70`). serde has no specialisation for `Vec<u8>`, so it goes through `VecVisitor::visit_seq` and bincode decodes the ~2.3 MB blob one `u8` at a time. Profile of the load path (macOS `sample`, upstream `4efbec1`):

| Frame | Share of `load_defaults_newlines` |
|---|---|
| `VecVisitor::visit_seq` -> `SeqAccess::next_element` | 67% |
| `deserialize_map` (`variables`) | 25% |
| `deserialize_string` | 21% |

On top of that, `from_uncompressed_data(&[u8])` goes through bincode's `IoReader`, which zero-fills and copies a temporary buffer for every string.

## Proposed fix

- Serialize/deserialize the field as bytes (`serialize_bytes` / `deserialize_byte_buf`, with a `visit_seq` fallback for formats that encode bytes as sequences). bincode encodes `&[u8]` and `Vec<u8>` identically (u64 length + raw bytes), so existing dumps, including ones made by downstream crates, keep loading and re-serialize byte-identical.
- Use `bincode::deserialize(slice)` in `from_uncompressed_data`, which uses the same bincode options as `deserialize_from`.

Measured on a prototype: warm load 1.81 ms -> 0.68 ms, `syncat` on a small file 11.7 ms -> 10.3 ms (median).

issue.title: perf: completion responses repeat the same edit range and commit characters on every item
issue.body:
## Problem

Completion responses repeat the same data on every item. With an `insertReplaceSupport` client, a global completion in a typical React project returns about 1000 items. Each one carries an identical `insert`/`replace` range pair and an identical `commitCharacters` array, which comes to about 300 bytes per item:

```json
{"label":"activeBar","kind":6,"sortText":"11","data":{"cacheId":1},
 "commitCharacters":[".",",",";","("],
 "textEdit":{"newText":"activeBar",
   "insert":{"start":{"line":1217,"character":2},"end":{"line":1217,"character":5}},
   "replace":{"start":{"line":1217,"character":2},"end":{"line":1217,"character":5}}}}
```

Completion is requested while typing, so the editor has to receive and parse all of this on almost every keystroke.

## Evidence

Measured on `recharts` with TypeScript 6.0.3:

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Items in a global completion response | 1068 |
| Mean response size | 317 KB |
| Bytes sent to the client over 110 typed characters with completion | 34 MB |
| Neovim `vim.json.decode` per response | 2.3 ms |

## Proposed fix

LSP 3.17 added `CompletionList.itemDefaults`, which clients opt into through `textDocument.completion.completionList.itemDefaults`. VS Code, Neovim ≥ 0.10, nvim-cmp and blink.cmp all support it. When the client supports `editRange` and `commitCharacters` defaults:

- send the shared edit range and commit characters once in `itemDefaults`;
- omit them from the items that match;
- use `textEditText` only where the inserted text differs from the label.

Responses for clients that don't opt in stay unchanged. Prototype result: 317 KB → 85 KB per response.

issue.title: perf: didChange re-scans the whole document for every content change
issue.body:
## Problem

Every content change in `textDocument/didChange` rebuilds the server-side `TextDocument` from scratch, so applying N changes re-scans the whole file N times. This is noticeable whenever the editor sends many changes at once: format on save, organize imports, rename, code actions, multi-cursor edits.

`LspDocument.applyEdit` (`src/document.ts`) does:

```ts
const start = this.offsetAt(change.range.start); // recomputes line offsets of the whole file
const end = this.offsetAt(change.range.end);
newContent = content.substr(0, start) + change.text + content.substr(end);
this._document = TextDocument.create(...);      // throws the line offsets away again
```

`TextDocument.create` discards the line index, so the next `offsetAt` calls `computeLineOffsets` over the whole document again. The cost is O(changes × file size).

## Evidence

A CPU profile of the server while it receives a `didChange` with 300 small edits on a 1.6k-line file (`recharts/src/cartesian/Bar.tsx`):

| Frame | Self time |
|---|---|
| `computeLineOffsets` | 492 ms of 532 ms total (93%) |

Measured cost: about 70 ms of language server CPU per such change. A single keystroke pays the same full rescan (about 0.35 ms on that file), and the cost grows linearly with file size.

## Proposed fix

Use `TextDocument.update(document, [change], version)` from `vscode-languageserver-textdocument`. It applies the change and updates the line offsets incrementally.

issue.title: perf: escape/unescape regexes dominate expand() on typical patterns
issue.body:
## Summary

`expand()` spends ~45% of its time in `escapeBraces` / `unescapeBraces`, even though almost every real pattern (`**/*.{js,ts}`, `src/{lib,bin}/**`) contains nothing to escape. Each call runs 5 `String#replace` regex passes on the input and 5 more on **every** result, and all of them are no-ops unless the input has a `\` (or a result contains the internal `\0` sentinels).

Since `minimatch` calls `expand()` for every pattern containing braces, this sits on the path of every glob construction.

## Evidence

- `src/index.ts:49-63`: `escapeBraces` / `unescapeBraces` always run all 5 replaces.
- `src/index.ts:140-148`: `escapeBraces` once per call, `unescapeBraces` once per result (`.map(unescapeBraces)`).

CPU profile (`node --cpu-prof`) over 12 typical glob patterns, self time:

| Frame | Self % |
|---|---|
| `unescapeBraces` | 26.6% |
| `escapeBraces` | 9.0% |
| 5 sentinel `RegExp`s (`\0SLASH…`, `\0OPEN…`, …) | ~8.5% |
| everything else (`parseCommaParts`, `expand_`, `range`, `combine`, GC, …) | ~56% |

## Proposed fix

Return early when there's nothing to replace:

- `escapeBraces`: skip if `str.indexOf('\\') === -1` (every escape pattern starts with a backslash);
- `unescapeBraces`: skip if `str.indexOf('\0') === -1` (every sentinel contains `\0`).

Output is unchanged. Measured: `expand()` ~1250 ns → ~670 ns per call (-47%), `new Minimatch()` -11%. PR incoming.

issue.title: minimatch() spends more time on its cache key than on matching
issue.body:
`minimatch(path, pattern)` spends more time looking up its cached `Minimatch` than matching the path, and `minimatch.filter()` is slower than `minimatch()`. The README says it is "still a bit faster".

### Evidence

CPU profile of 150k `minimatch(f, p)` calls on 11.0.5 (`ea0a4a6`), with 15 everyday globs over `benchmark/realistic-paths.json`:

| self time | function |
|---|---|
| **46%** | `cachedMinimatch` (`src/index.ts:130`) |
| 10% | `Matcher#test` |
| 6% | `Minimatch#match` |

Each call builds `pattern + '\0' + JSON.stringify(options)` (`src/index.ts:131`). V8 then flattens and hashes that new string for the `Map.get`. A cache hit also does a `delete` + `set` to keep the LRU order.

`filter()` (`src/index.ts:167-170`) calls `minimatch()` for each path, so it pays for the same lookup and also goes through a closure.

### Cost

15,505 paths × 10 globs (`**/*.js`, `**/*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,mts,cts}`, `**/node_modules/**`, ...). Each figure is the median of 5 process runs, each of those the median of 15 rounds:

| API | ms |
|---|---|
| `Minimatch#match` | 14.5 |
| `minimatch(f, p)` | 37.3 (2.6x the `Minimatch#match` time) |
| `minimatch(f, p, { dot: true })` | 40.0 |
| `minimatch.filter(p)` | 49.2 |

### Proposed fix

- Key the cache by options first, then by pattern. The user's pattern string keeps its hash, so there is no concatenated key to hash. With no options, use a constant key and skip `JSON.stringify`.
- Use two generations (as quick-lru does) in place of an exact LRU, so a hit is two `Map.get`s with no reordering. Each object used within the last 256 inserts is still kept.
- `filter()` makes its `Minimatch` once, the first time it tests a path.

issue.title: Reduce per-keystroke highlighting latency
issue.body:
## Summary

Reduces per-keystroke highlighting latency by 33-48% (p50) on typical command lines on my machine. Highlighting output is unchanged.

Note: my machine runs endpoint security agents that make file opens slow (`open("/dev/null")` + `close` costs 60µs in plain C). That inflates the redirection costs below, so on a clean system the gain will be smaller. The `sysread` gain does not depend on it and was reproduced by @ccjmne on another machine (21-45%).

The line counting fix and the daemon exit on early disconnect, originally part of this PR, were merged in #114 and #115.

Most of the time per keystroke went to the Zsh client, not the daemon: for a typical command line, the daemon needs 80-290µs while the whole round trip took 0.5-1.5ms.

## Where the time went

| Cost per keystroke | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `zsocket ... 2>/dev/null` | ~200µs | ~25µs |
| `{ print ... } >&$fd` when sending the request | ~120µs | single `print -u` |
| Reading spans with `read -r` (one byte per syscall) | ~8µs per span | one bulk `sysread` |
| First highlight of a new construct after daemon start | up to 1.5ms | ~0.2ms |

On my machine (macOS, zsh 5.9), any redirection on a builtin costs ~120µs, regardless of shell options, mostly because of the slow `open()`:

```
:                       3.6us
: 2>/dev/null         138.3us
: 2>&$fd               75.8us
: 2>&-                 28.9us
```

## Changes

**Client (`templates/zsh-patina.zsh`)**

- Remove the redirections from the hot path
- Send the request with a single write, and answer each CAL/NMD query with a single write
- After the first span line, read the rest of the response with `sysread` and split it into lines (see the discussion below about the protocol specification)

**Daemon (`src/daemon.rs`)**

- Wrap the response writer in a `BufWriter`. The query functions already flush before reading an answer, so the protocol is unchanged.
- Warm up with a command line that touches many more syntax contexts. Syntect compiles regexes lazily, so the first use of a construct (quotes, `$(...)`, loops, heredocs, etc.) took up to 1.5ms. The warm-up runs in the background and costs ~44ms more CPU at startup.

## Results

`main` vs this PR, client and daemon, called alternately with the same buffer, median of 400 runs, macOS, zsh 5.9:

| Command | Spans | `main` | This PR | Gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ls` | 1 | 376µs | 212µs | 44% |
| `echo hello world` | 2 | 401µs | 244µs | 39% |
| `carg` (missing command) | 1 | 657µs | 365µs | 44% |
| `git commit -m "..." && cargo build ... \| tail -3` | 20 | 808µs | 457µs | 43% |
| `for f in ~/Documents/*.txt; do ...; done` | 31 | 868µs | 451µs | 48% |
| long `docker run ...` | 13 | 794µs | 532µs | 33% |

A second run gave 35-48%.

## Testing

- `cargo test`
- `region_highlight` output is identical to `main` in 29 end-to-end cases: aliases (including recursive ones), named directories, multi-line buffers, `PREBUFFER`, active region, Unicode, history expansion

## Trade-off

If the daemon dies but leaves its socket file behind, `zsocket` now prints its own error to stderr in addition to the existing `zle -M` message. This only affects that failure path.

## AI usage

Claude Code (Opus 5.5) built profiling harnesses and helped with profiling, then reviewed the code and ran a parallel run of the benchmarks to ensure results matched with manual ones.

issue.title: Semantic tokens re-check files on a cold query checker after diagnostics already checked them

labels.name: repo-0441092b
labels.description: Constraints of the existing architecture prevent this from being fixed

issue.body:
### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

**Summary:** after every edit, the language server type-checks the edited file twice. Diagnostics check it on the dedicated diagnostics checker. Semantic tokens then re-infer most of the same types on a fresh query checker, because `reclassifyByType` calls `GetTypeAtLocation` for every variable, property and parameter (`ls/semantictokens.go:421`). On a real component file that's ~40 ms of extra CPU per semantic tokens request. I'd like to know whether reusing the diagnostics checker, once it has finished with the file, fits the checker pool design.

**Measurements** (`main` @ f7973164a, Apple M1 Pro, recharts `src/cartesian/Line.tsx`: 1,093 lines in a 658-file program; 120 keystrokes, 3 runs)

| Request | median |
|---|---|
| `textDocument/diagnostic` | 52.6–53.2 ms |
| `textDocument/semanticTokens/full` on a cold query checker | 41.3–41.7 ms |
| the same request again on the now-warm query checker | ~2 ms |

About 28 ms of each semantic tokens request is first-touch type inference: destructured props, `const` initializers that are calls, large annotation types. It's all local to the file, so I couldn't find a per-token shortcut that keeps the classification identical.

**Why reuse would usually apply:** VS Code pulls diagnostics as soon as a document changes (`diagnosticPullOptions.onChange: true` in `packages/vscode-typescript/src/client.ts`). It requests semantic tokens at least 300 ms after a content change (`REQUEST_MIN_DELAY = 300` in vscode's `documentSemanticTokens.ts`). So by the time semantic tokens arrive, the diagnostics checker has normally finished with the file.

**What I tried** (branch: hood/TypeScript `perf/semantic-tokens`, +116/−5)

The pool lends the diagnostics checker to a semantic tokens request only when all of these hold:
- the checker is idle (non-blocking `diagSem`);
- it has fully checked the file (type check and unused check, not cancelled);
- no diagnostics request for that file is still in flight.

The in-flight guard is needed because a diagnostics request uses the checker three times (semantic, suggestion and declaration diagnostics) and releases it in between. In every other case the request gets a query checker exactly as today, and it never waits. So queries never run on the diagnostics checker before or during a file's diagnostics, and the order in which the checker walks the file is unchanged. That ordering is what prevents bugs like #51661, where a query asked for a type before the normal walk and the result was an order-dependent false implicit-any in the editor.

| recharts `Line.tsx`, 120 keystrokes, 3 runs | `main` | branch |
|---|---|---|
| Diagnostics, then semantic tokens: semantic tokens median | 41.3–41.7 ms | 2.88–2.91 ms |
| Same: diagnostics median | 52.6–53.2 ms | 52.4–52.9 ms |
| Same: process CPU | 14.5–14.7 s | 8.6 s (−41%) |
| Both requests sent at once: keystroke median / CPU | 53–55 ms / 14.7 s | 54 ms / 14.7 s (falls back, no change) |

Correctness so far:
- Semantic tokens and diagnostics for `Line.tsx` and three other open files are byte-identical to `main` across 600 responses, both sequential and concurrent. That includes TS2883 errors that print types, unused-variable suggestions, and the transient errors you get mid-typing.
- `hereby test`, `lint` and `check:format` pass.
- The new pool test fails if the in-flight guard is removed.

**The part I'm not sure about:** after the file is checked, the classification queries still create a few types and symbols on the diagnostics checker (~6 types and 32 symbols per request here). Most likely these are throwaway re-checks of expressions. I saw no change in any diagnostics, but I can't prove that holds for every program. If keeping that checker completely free of query work is a hard requirement, this approach doesn't fit, and I'd be glad to hear whether another direction would be welcome.

I worked on this with help from an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). I've reviewed the change, and I'll handle any follow-up myself.

On its own, `await import('unifont')` takes ~165-190 ms here (most of it css-tree + mdn-data).

css-tree is also pulled in by SVGO through `astro/config` (#18655), so both need fixing before css-tree drops out entirely. With both fixed, measured on a 400-post Markdown blog with no fonts and no SVGs:

| `import('astro/config')` | 905 modules | 634 | 496 |

| css-tree / unifont / svgo modules loaded during build | 358 | 130 | 0 |

When `fonts` isn't configured, no font resolution dependencies are loaded:

- `fontProviders.*()` uses its literal provider name and loads unifont in `init()`. `test/units/assets/fonts/providers.test.ts` already pins those names.
- `fontsPlugin.buildStart` returns early when there are no fonts (matching `buildEnd`), and loads the unifont/capsize resolvers on demand.

issue.body:
## Summary

The router builds a fresh stats measurement with `stats.Default.NewTaggedStat(...)` for every delivered job, five times per job:

| Stat | Where (`f51e4ca`) | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| `delivery_latency` | `router/worker.go:462` | per request |
| `router_delivery_payload_size_bytes` | `router/worker.go:598` | per request |
| `router_response_counts` | `router/worker.go:1095` | per job |
| `event_delivery` | `router/worker.go:1113` | per delivered job |
| `event_delivery_time` | `router/worker.go:1125` | per delivered job |

Each call allocates a tags map, sanitizes every tag key, builds a sorted key string plus `fmt.Sprintf("%f", samplingRate)` (statsd) or a canonical attribute set (OTel), and takes a shared lock to find the client/instrument. The set of distinct tag combinations is small and stable, so all of this is repeated work.

## Cost

Measured on go-kit v0.86.0, Apple M1 Pro, one stat with the `router_response_counts` tag set:

| Backend | `NewTaggedStat` per call | Cached measurement |
|---|---|---|
| statsd (default) | 3.0 µs, 1.2 KB, 11 allocs | 0.72 µs, 0 allocs |
| OTel/Prometheus | 2.8 µs, 1.5 KB, 9 allocs | 0.41 µs, 1 alloc |

With 8 goroutines the uncached statsd path stays at ~3.0 µs/op, so it doesn't scale with cores.

For the three stats emitted per successfully delivered job (`sendEventDeliveryStat` + `sendRouterResponseCountStat`) that is **9.8 µs, 3.4 KB and 34 allocations per job**.

## Proposal

Use the existing `utils/cache.StatsCache` (already used in the same file for `transformer_outgoing_request_*`), keyed by comparable label structs, so a measurement is built once per tag combination. Emitted metric names and tags stay exactly the same.

issue.title: LSP messages are JSON-encoded twice when written to the client

labels.name: repo-0441092b
labels.description: This issue needs a team member to investigate its status.

issue.body:
### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

**Summary:** every message the language server sends is JSON-encoded twice. `lsproto.Message` only implements the `[]byte`-returning `MarshalJSON`, so `encoding/json/v2` takes the already-encoded bytes and re-validates and copies them into the outer encoder. On a large completion response this costs about a third of the encode time and well over half of its allocations.

**Where**

- `tsc/internal/lsp/server.go:156`: `lspWriter.Write` calls `json.Marshal(msg)`.
- `tsc/internal/lsp/lsproto/jsonrpc.go:76`: `(*Message).MarshalJSON` returns `json.Marshal(m.msg)`.
- json/v2 then runs `jsontext.(*Encoder).WriteValue` over the returned bytes (`reformatObject` / `reformatArray` in profiles).

**Measured** (Apple M1 Pro, `main` @ f7973164a)

| Workload | `main` | `MarshalJSONTo` | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encode a 2,000-item completion response (time, benchstat n=10) | 1.934 ms ±7% | 1.273 ms ±1% | −34.2% (p=0.000) |
| Same (B/op) | 1243 KiB | 467 KiB | −62.5% |
| Same (allocs/op) | 37 | 16 | −57% |
| Real global completion in recharts `src/cartesian/Line.tsx` (1,916 items, 531 KB) | 2.93 ms | 1.89 ms | −36% |

The cost applies to every response and notification. It matters most for completions, semantic tokens and diagnostics, which are large and are sent on almost every keystroke.

**Proposed fix**

Implement `json.MarshalerTo` on `Message` so the wrapped message is encoded straight into the encoder:

```go
func (m *Message) MarshalJSONTo(enc *json.Encoder) error {
	return json.MarshalEncode(enc, m.msg)
}
```

The output is byte-identical. I checked it against `main` on the 531 KB payload and on responses with invalid UTF-8, HTML characters, null results and errors. The full `hereby test` suite, `hereby lint` and `check:format` pass. I have a branch ready with this change, an equivalence test and a benchmark, and I'm happy to open a PR if you'd like it (I already have the code ready on a branch in my fork: https://github.com/hood/TypeScript/tree/perf/lsp-message-marshal).

I found and patched this with help from an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). I've reviewed the change and will handle any follow-up myself.

issue.title: perf(tarball): hash the decoded tar while its files are written
issue.body:
## Summary

On the eager extraction path (`extract_gzipped_tarball_with_tar`), the extraction thread blocks in `cas_write_pool().install(...)` while the pool writes the package's files. Afterwards it runs `eager_tar_integrity`, which computes a CRC32 and a SHA-512 over the whole decoded tar. That pass is serial and comes after the writes, so it adds directly to each package's extraction time.

The tar hash costs about as much as decompression. On 6 real npm tarballs (63 MB of tar), SHA-512 of the tar took 87 ms on one core, while zune-inflate took 67 ms.

## Proposed fix

Run the tar hash on the extraction thread while the pool writes the files (`ThreadPool::in_place_scope`). The thread is idle during the writes anyway, so the pool gets no extra work. Output is unchanged.

## Measurements

- Machine: M1 Pro, macOS.
- Method: per-package extraction into a fresh store, old and new path interleaved in one binary, median of 10 runs.

| Package | Before | After | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| typescript 5.6.3 | 67.5 ms | 47.4 ms | −30% |
| react-dom 18.3.1 | 14.8 ms | 10.4 ms | −30% |
| date-fns 4.1.0 | 376 ms | 346 ms | −8% |
| lodash 4.17.21 | 85.2 ms | 80.7 ms | −5% |
| rxjs 7.8.1 | 176 ms | 173 ms | −2% |
| `@babel/core` 7.26.0 | 14.6 ms | 14.6 ms | 0% |

Packages with fewer than 32 files are written serially on the extraction thread, so they do not overlap and do not gain. On a whole install the gain is smaller where per-file syscalls dominate, such as macOS with endpoint security software.

issue.title: perf(deps-restorer): skip the mode alignment after a reflink when the source mode is known
issue.body:
## Summary

On macOS, every file the clone tier imports is followed by an `open`, `fstat`, and `close` of the new file to align its mode (`align_target_mode` → `set_path_permissions` in `deps-restorer/src/link_file.rs`). A reflink already gives the target the source's mode, and the install usually knows the source's mode from when it wrote or verified the store file (`StoreFile::mode()`). When that mode is the desired one, the extra `open` changes nothing.

The cost is large where `open` is expensive, such as macOS machines running endpoint security software. Those machines intercept every `open`. The link pool on macOS has 4 threads, so this work is on the critical path.

## Measurements

- Machine: M1 Pro, macOS, endpoint security active.
- Fixture: the integrated-benchmark fixture (~1,350 packages).
- Command: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against registry.npmjs.org.
- Method: same binary, behavior switched by an env var, 5 interleaved rounds.

| Scenario | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cold store and cache | 14.6 s | 10.4 s (−29%) |
| Warm store, no `node_modules` | 2.46 s | 2.27 s |

Profile of the cold install (`sample`, samples whose top frame is a syscall):

| Call site | Samples |
| --- | --- |
| `open` in store writes (`FileCreation::open`) | 3,104 |
| `clonefileat` in `clone_tier` | 1,780 |
| `close` in store writes | 1,394 |
| `open` in `file_equals_bytes` | 1,156 |
| **`open` + `close` in `set_path_permissions`** | **1,208** |
| SHA-512 (`compress512`) | 206 |

The modes of all 73,605 files in `node_modules` and `<store>/links` were identical with and without the skip.

## Proposed fix

Skip the alignment after a reflink when `StoreFile::mode()` is known and equals the desired mode. Keep it when the mode is unknown or differs, and in `recover_from_concurrent_import`, where the target may not be a reflink of the source.

comment.body: pnpm/pnpm#17766 implements the proposed fix in full. The clone tier skips the mode alignment when the install already read the source's mode as the desired one. It still aligns when the mode is unknown or differs, and in the concurrent-import recovery path.

issue.title: Ok/Err passthrough methods allocate needless copies
issue.body:
## Summary
Methods that don't apply their callback still allocate a copy of the result: `Err.map`, `Err.andThen`, `Err.andThrough`, `Err.andTee`, `Err.orTee`, `Ok.mapErr`, `Ok.orElse`, `Ok.orTee`, `Ok.andTee`. `Ok.andThrough` also allocates a closure plus an extra `Ok` via `.map(() => this.value)`.

Since `Ok`/`Err` are immutable (`readonly value` / `readonly error`), returning `this` is equivalent and allocation-free.

## Measurements
| Benchmark | Time |
|---|---|
| `err('e')` through 10 skipped steps | 4.4ns |

V8 escape analysis removes some of these in microbenchmarks, so real-world GC savings in long pipelines are likely higher than this shows.

## Proposal
Return `this` (cast where the phantom type parameter changes) on all passthrough branches.

issue.title: ResultAsync.combine passes thenables to Promise.all
issue.body:
## Summary
`ResultAsync.combine` and `combineWithAllErrors` pass `ResultAsync` instances to `Promise.all`. They are thenables, not native promises, so each element goes through `NewPromiseResolveThenableJob`: one extra promise and one extra tick per element. The result is then re-wrapped via `fromSafePromise(...).andThen(...)`, adding more ticks.

```ts
ResultAsync.fromSafePromise(Promise.all(asyncResultList)).andThen(combineResultList)
```

## Measurements
| Benchmark | Ticks to settle | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `ResultAsync.combine` of 10k | 6 | 2.22ms |

## Proposal
Pass the underlying `_promise`s to `Promise.all` (accessible from the static methods on `ResultAsync`) and `.then(combineResultList)` directly.

issue.title: Result.combine allocates a closure and an Ok per element
issue.body:
## Summary
`combineResultList` (used by `Result.combine` and `ResultAsync.combine`) allocates a closure and a new `Ok` for every element:

```ts
// src/_internals/utils.ts
acc.map((list) => list.push(result.value))  // new closure + new Ok(list.length) per element
```

## Measurements
| Benchmark | Time |
|---|---|
| `Result.combine` of 10k `Ok` | 33.1µs |

## Proposal
Plain indexed loop into a pre-sized array, early-return on the first `Err`.

issue.title: ResultAsync steps cost ~3 microtask ticks instead of 1
issue.body:
## Summary
Each `ResultAsync` step (`map`, `mapErr`, `orElse`) costs ~3 microtask ticks instead of 1, because the `.then` callback is an `async` function and `await f(x)` adds a tick even when `f` is sync. The Err/Ok passthrough branches also allocate a fresh `Err`/`Ok` per step.

```ts
// src/result-async.ts
this._promise.then(async (res) => {
  if (res.isErr()) return new Err(res.error)   // copy
  return new Ok(await f(res.value))            // extra promise + tick even for sync f
})
```

## Measurements
Chain: `okAsync(1).map(inc).map(inc).map(inc).mapErr(inc).andThen(ok).map(inc).orElse(err).map(inc).map(inc).map(inc).map(inc)`

| | Microtask ticks to settle | Time per chain |
|---|---|---|
| 11-step Ok chain | 32 | 1.67µs |
| 6-step Err chain | 17 | n/a |

## Proposal
Use a plain (non-async) `.then` callback, call `f` directly and only chain when it returns a thenable; pass the existing `Result` through on the skipped branch.

issue.title: perf(#3384): skip fnamemodify in is_git when GIT_DIR unset
issue.body:
In `explorer/watch.lua`, `is_git` executes for every directory node assigned a filesystem watcher. 

Previously, even when `GIT_DIR` was unset, the function invoked expensive Vimscript evaluations, calling `vim.fn.fnamemodify(path, ":p")`, `fnamemodify(nil, ":p")`, and `fnamemodify(path, ":t")` on every check 🫠 .

- `is_git` across ~1,5k directories dropped from ~130 ms down to ~2.5 ms (~50x speedup) (!!)
- Output remains 1:1 with that’s currently running on master

*AI usage*: Claude Code (Opus 5.5) helped on self-review, code cleanup and most importantly measuring the impact.

Tested on macOS nvim-dev 0.13, untested on Windows (though `path_basename` relies on `package.config` path separators), Linux, Neovim 0.10/0.11, and scenarios where `GIT_DIR` is explicitly defined.

```rust
const PUMP_INTERVAL: f64 = 0.016;
NSTimer::scheduledTimerWithTimeInterval_repeats_block(PUMP_INTERVAL, true, &block)
```

## Impact

Tray idle (`perf/idle.bench.ts#window-closed`, `cpu.wakes`), window idle, and `listening-at-rest` all pay for it. By my count it's about 75% of the tray's timer wakeups.

## Expected

Tick every frame only while the HUD animates. Otherwise, idle at a slow pace and let whatever sends the pump something (HUD events, menu actions, `hex` control calls, input-source changes) wake it at once.
